country.name: Belgium
country.tagline: A beer country quietly rebuilding a medieval wine tradition, with Chardonnay and Crémant on Meuse slopes and Flemish hills.

stats.note: Statbel via FAOSTAT (official figure): 900 ha of vines in 2024, up from 680 ha in 2023. No reliable current production figure: FAOSTAT's Belgian wine numbers are estimates; production was about 4,000 hl in 2006 and has grown strongly since. See gaps

country.overview:
Belgium had vineyards long before it became famous for beer. Monks of the Carolingian era planted vines around Liège and Huy on the Meuse, and Leuven had 23 public wine presses in 1411. The Little Ice Age, cheap Burgundy, wars and the rise of beer ended most of that, and by the nineteenth century the country was better known for table grapes grown under glass in the Hoeilaart greenhouses near Brussels.

The modern revival began in the 1960s and accelerated with warmer summers. Belgium now has seven protected designations, four in Flanders and three in Wallonia, and a few hundred hectares of vines. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris grow alongside Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau and fungus-resistant varieties such as Johanniter and Solaris. Sparkling wine, especially Crémant de Wallonie, is the strongest suit, and estates such as Domaine du Chant d'Eole near Mons and Ruffus (Domaine des Agaises) at Haulchin have won international awards with traditional-method wines from chalk soils that continue those of Champagne. In Flanders, Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen in Haspengouw and Wijndomein Aldeneyck in the Maas valley are the best-known names.

history.title: Monastic vineyards on the Meuse
history.text: Vineyards at Vivegnis near Liège and at Huy were already old in the ninth century; part of the Huy vineyard belonged to the Bishop of Liège.

history.title: Leuven's 23 presses
history.text: At its medieval peak the city of Leuven had 23 public wine presses, a sign of how widespread viticulture was in Brabant.

history.title: Grapes under glass
history.text: From 1862 table grapes were grown in greenhouses around Hoeilaart and Overijse; by 1960 there were about 35,000.

history.title: Appellations return
history.text: Hageland became Belgium's first wine appellation in 1997, followed by Haspengouw, Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Heuvelland, Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn and, in 2008 to 2009, Crémant de Wallonie and Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie.

country.classification: Seven PDOs: in Flanders Hagelandse wijn, Haspengouwse wijn, Heuvellandse wijn and Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn; in Wallonia Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Crémant de Wallonie and Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie. The cross-border Maasvallei Limburg PDO (2017) is shared with the Netherlands. PGIs are Vlaamse landwijn and Vin de pays des Jardins de Wallonie. National dates (1997 to 2009) and EU registration dates differ; the EU register lists Hagelandse and Haspengouwse wijn from 2004.
country.climate_soils: Cool maritime to slightly continental. Chalk and marl in Hainaut (continuous with Champagne's chalk), loess in Haspengouw and Hageland, iron-rich sandstone (ijzerzandsteen) hills in Hageland, sandy and gravelly soils in the Maas valley, and clay hills in Heuvelland near the French border.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: The most acclaimed variety, for still and sparkling.

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs (registration dates, varieties, communes)

regions.name: Wallonia
regions.tagline: Chalk slopes of Hainaut and the Meuse valley, home of Crémant de Wallonie.
regions.summary: Wallonia's vineyards are concentrated in Hainaut near Mons and Binche, the Sambre and Meuse valleys around Namur, Dinant and Huy, and near Liège. The three Walloon PDOs cover still wine (Côtes de Sambre et Meuse) and sparkling wine (Crémant de Wallonie, Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie) across the whole region.
regions.history: The Meuse valley at Huy and Liège had vineyards from Carolingian times. Château de Bioul near Anhée revived a historic estate in the 2000s.
regions.terroir: Chalk and marl in Hainaut, slate and limestone in the Meuse valley.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Johanniter, Solaris.
regions.classification: Three PDOs: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Crémant de Wallonie, Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie; PGI Vin de pays des Jardins de Wallonie.
appellations: Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs (registration dates, varieties, communes)

regions.name: Flanders
regions.tagline: Haspengouw's loess, Hageland's ironstone hills and the Maas valley.
regions.summary: Flanders has four PDOs and shares a fifth with the Netherlands. Hageland in Flemish Brabant, on iron-rich sandstone hills around Aarschot, Diest and Leuven, was the first Belgian appellation in 1997; Haspengouw (Hesbaye) in Limburg is fruit-orchard country on loess; Heuvelland, near Ypres on the French border, is a small hilly area; and Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn covers Flemish sparkling wine. The Maasvallei Limburg PDO crosses the Maas into the Netherlands.
regions.history: Leuven's medieval presses and the Hageland's monastic vineyards are the historic roots.
regions.terroir: Loess, sand, ironstone and clay; cool maritime climate.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder, Regent, Johanniter.
regions.classification: PDOs: Hagelandse wijn, Haspengouwse wijn, Heuvellandse wijn, Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn, Maasvallei Limburg (with the Netherlands); PGI Vlaamse landwijn.

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs (registration dates, varieties, communes)

be-cotes-de-sambre-et-meuse.name: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse
be-cotes-de-sambre-et-meuse.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Regent, Johanniter and others
be-cotes-de-sambre-et-meuse.summary: Wallonia's still-wine PDO covers the valleys of the Sambre and Meuse and much of the surrounding provinces (199 municipalities in the EU register). It has the broadest grape list of any Belgian appellation, including Chasselas, Merlot, Regent, Johanniter and old Seibel hybrids, which reflects the experimental nature of Walloon viticulture.
be-cotes-de-sambre-et-meuse.terroir: Slate, limestone and alluvium on Meuse and Sambre slopes.
be-cotes-de-sambre-et-meuse.nerd_note: The cooperative Vin de Liège, founded in 2010, replanted the hills of the Meuse where Liège's medieval vineyards once stood.

be-cremant-de-wallonie.name: Crémant de Wallonie
be-cremant-de-wallonie.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc (white); Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier
be-cremant-de-wallonie.summary: Traditional-method sparkling wine from anywhere in Wallonia, with at least nine months on lees. Chalk soils in Hainaut give Crémant of real finesse, and Domaine du Chant d'Eole and Ruffus have won international medals.
be-cremant-de-wallonie.terroir: Chalk and marl in Hainaut; slate and limestone in the Meuse valley.
be-cremant-de-wallonie.nerd_note: Chant d'Eole stands among wind turbines, which gave the estate its name ('song of the wind').

be-hagelandse-wijn.name: Hagelandse wijn
be-hagelandse-wijn.grapes: Chardonnay, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, Pinot Noir, Dornfelder and others
be-hagelandse-wijn.summary: Hageland, east of Leuven in Flemish Brabant, was Belgium's first modern wine appellation in 1997. Its rolling hills of iron-rich sandstone (ijzerzandsteen) around Aarschot, Diest, Tienen and Hoegaarden, a region once dotted with medieval vineyards, give fresh whites and light reds. Yields are capped at 67 hl/ha.
be-hagelandse-wijn.terroir: Ferruginous sandstone hills, sand and loam.
be-hagelandse-wijn.nerd_note: The Hageland's ironstone was also the building stone of its Gothic churches.

be-haspengouwse-wijn.name: Haspengouwse wijn
be-haspengouwse-wijn.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Riesling and others
be-haspengouwse-wijn.summary: Haspengouw, the fruit-orchard country of Belgian Limburg around Sint-Truiden, Borgloon and Tongeren, has deep loess soils over chalk and is home to Belgium's best-known winery, Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen at Riemst, whose Chardonnay is aged in oak.
be-haspengouwse-wijn.terroir: Loess over chalk and marl; gentle slopes.
be-haspengouwse-wijn.nerd_note: Clos d'Opleeuw near Borgloon makes a Chardonnay sometimes compared to good Burgundy.

be-heuvellandse-wijn.name: Heuvellandse wijn
be-heuvellandse-wijn.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Johanniter, Regent and others
be-heuvellandse-wijn.summary: A small appellation in the West Flemish hills near Kemmel and Dranouter, close to the French border and the First World War battlefields of Ypres. Wijngoed Monteberg and Entre-Deux-Monts are the best-known estates.
be-heuvellandse-wijn.terroir: Clay and sand hills of the Flemish heights.
be-heuvellandse-wijn.nerd_note: Heuvelland's vineyards grow on ground fought over in the First World War.

be-maasvallei-limburg.name: Maasvallei Limburg
be-maasvallei-limburg.grapes: Auxerrois, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Siegerrebe, Pinot Noir, Dornfelder, Acolon
be-maasvallei-limburg.summary: Maasvallei Limburg is the first cross-border PDO in the EU: 11 municipalities on both banks of the Maas, in Belgian Limburg (Maaseik, Kinrooi, Dilsen-Stokkem, Maasmechelen, Lanaken) and Dutch Limburg (Maasgouw, Echt-Susteren, Roermond, Leudal, Sittard-Geleen, Stein). Gravel and sand terraces deposited by the river give crisp whites; Wijndomein Aldeneyck at Maaseik and Wijngoed Thorn are key producers.
be-maasvallei-limburg.terroir: Maas river gravel, sand and loam terraces; mild climate in the river valley.
be-maasvallei-limburg.nerd_note: Thorn, the Dutch 'white village', gave its name to Wijngoed Thorn on the Dutch bank.

be-vin-mousseux-de-qualite-de-wallonie.name: Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie
be-vin-mousseux-de-qualite-de-wallonie.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris and others
be-vin-mousseux-de-qualite-de-wallonie.summary: A broader Walloon sparkling-wine PDO than Crémant, allowing more grape varieties and less strict methods, used for quality sparkling wines that fall outside the Crémant rules.

be-vlaamse-mousserende-kwaliteitswijn.name: Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn
be-vlaamse-mousserende-kwaliteitswijn.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Riesling
be-vlaamse-mousserende-kwaliteitswijn.summary: The PDO for quality sparkling wine from the whole of Flanders (300 municipalities in the EU register), registered nationally in 2005. It allows the Champagne and Pinot family grapes plus Auxerrois and Riesling, and is used by most Flemish estates that make traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: Domaine du Chant d'Eole
sites.text: An estate at Quévy near Mons planted from 2010 on chalk among wind turbines, now Belgium's most famous sparkling-wine producer.

sites.name: Ruffus (Domaine des Agaises)
sites.text: Raymond Leroy's estate at Haulchin near Binche, planted from 2002 on chalk with Champagne grapes, a pioneer of Belgian sparkling wine.

sites.name: Château de Bioul
sites.class: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse / Crémant de Wallonie
sites.text: A castle estate near Anhée in the Meuse valley whose owners replanted vines and built a modern winery.

sites.name: Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen
sites.text: A castle estate at Riemst near Tongeren, Belgium's best-known and long its largest wine estate, with oak-aged Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Wijndomein Aldeneyck
sites.text: An estate at Aldeneik near Maaseik on the Maas gravel terraces, one of the leading Flemish producers.

sites.name: Wijngoed Monteberg
sites.text: A vineyard on the slopes of the Monteberg at Dranouter in the Heuvelland hills, close to the French border and the First World War front.
